reading.rtitle: Writing to an American Program -- A Guide for International Graduates
paras: THE SUBJECT LINE. A program coordinator may receive two hundred emails a day. Therefore, your subject line has to say who you are and what you need: Observership application -- Diego Wached -- documents attached. A subject line like Question or Hello is easy to ignore.

ONE EMAIL, ONE PURPOSE. Start with Dear Dr. Smith or Dear Ms. Lopez, never with Hi or with no name. In the first sentence, say why you are writing: I am writing regarding... Ask for one thing only. Although it is tempting to ask five questions at once, a long email usually gets a short answer, or no answer at all.

THE REGISTER. American emails are polite, but they are also direct. Many Brazilian doctors write very long introductions; however, a coordinator prefers three short paragraphs. Use Could you please... and I would appreciate it if... instead of I need or I want. If the matter is urgent, say why, and add the deadline.

THE FOLLOW-THROUGH. Attach every document that you mention, and check the attachment before you click Send. If you do not receive an answer in a week, send a short, friendly reminder. Close with Thank you for your time and Kind regards, followed by your full name, as a result of which nobody has to guess who you are.

listenings.text: I coordinate a dermatology residency program, and on a busy day I receive about two hundred emails. So I read them in a very practical order. First, I look at the subject line. If it has a full name and says what the person needs, I open it. If it says Question, or Hello, I usually leave it for later, and later often means never. Second, I look at the greeting. Dear Ms. Lopez tells me that you read our website. Hi, with no name, tells me that you sent the same email to fifty programs. Third, I look at the length. Although I want to help everybody, I cannot answer an email with five questions in one paragraph. However, if you ask me one clear question, I can answer in thirty seconds. And please, attach the document that you mention. Every week, somebody writes Please find attached my CV, and there is no CV. As a result, I have to write back, and the conversation takes two weeks instead of two days.

The first email I wrote to an American attending was a disaster, and I am glad I never sent it. It was nine paragraphs long. I started with my medical school, my residency, my family, and my dream of living in the United States. Only in the last paragraph did I ask if I could observe her clinic. A friend who was already working in Boston read it and laughed. He said: she will stop reading after the second line. Therefore, I started again. I wrote a subject line with my name and the word observership. I wrote one paragraph about who I am, one paragraph with my request and the dates, and one short paragraph to thank her. Although I was worried that it sounded cold, my friend said it sounded professional. I attached my CV and checked the attachment twice. She answered the next morning, and she invited me to shadow her clinic for two weeks. As a result, I now write every important email in three paragraphs.

extra_audio.text: Dear Ms. Lopez, I am writing regarding my application for your observership program. Although I sent all my documents in May, my file is still pending. Could you please confirm if anything is missing? Thank you for your time. Kind regards, Diego Wached
